quizTarget: Change Ready to Changed, save, and run the same Rscript command again. Which message is produced?

essentialSupport.fact: Save the example as main.R and run Rscript --vanilla main.R. --vanilla avoids saved-workspace restoration and startup-profile customization; it does not install packages or make every external dependency identical.
cat writes supplied values as text. The string "\n" supplies a newline; print instead produces an R-style representation that can include index labels such as [1].

These fixtures run on R 4.5.0 with available base packages. Current official release manuals describe a newer release; this course does not claim the installed runtime is the latest version. The app is a concept reader, not an R browser runner.

reasoning: Rscript evaluates the saved file; a GUI and manual compilation are not required.

quizTarget: Replace the second value with "two". What type is reported?

essentialSupport.fact: c(1, 2) combines values into an atomic vector. Its elements share a common storage type; c is a function call, not a declaration of separate scalar variables.
Combining numeric values with text converts this atomic vector to character data. Logical values can be converted to numbers when combined with numeric values.
typeof(values) returns the storage type name. This is distinct from class, which can describe higher-level behavior such as a factor or data frame.

reasoning: This c call produces a single common atomic type; the character element makes the result character.

quizTarget: Remove L from 1L. What type prints?

essentialSupport.fact: 1 is normally a double-precision numeric value in R, even though it looks like a whole number.
1L creates an integer value. typeof distinguishes integer from double; both can participate in numeric calculations.
Double precision cannot represent every real number exactly. Integer storage has a finite range; neither type is an unlimited exact arithmetic guarantee.

reasoning: R normally represents an unsuffixed numeric literal as double.

quizTarget: Replace c(10,20) with the single value 10. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: For equal-length numeric vectors, + adds corresponding positions rather than concatenating them.
c(1,2,3,4) + c(10,20) repeats the shorter vector to match four positions. A non-multiple length can warn; a warning is not a validation policy.
Adding 10 to this vector adds ten to every entry. For unrelated data, check lengths explicitly instead of relying on accidental recycling.
cat(result, sep=",") prints entries separated by commas. sep controls formatting, not the calculation.

reasoning: The shorter operand now has one value, so every element receives the same increment.

quizTarget: Replace the right operand TRUE with FALSE. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: c(TRUE,FALSE) is a two-element logical vector. NA can represent an unknown logical value.
& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

if needs one non-missing logical result. A scalar numeric value can be coerced to logical, but explicit comparisons make intent clearer. It does not choose a policy for an entire vector or an unknown value.

reasoning: Elementwise AND with FALSE is false at both positions.

quizTarget: Change the index vector to c(2,3). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: values[1] selects the first element, not the second. Brackets request a subset.
values[c(1,3)] selects the first and third entries, in that requested order. Repeating an index can repeat an entry.
For this simple atomic vector, an absent positive position yields NA. Other extraction operators have different rules, taught later.

reasoning: R uses one-based positions and preserves the requested index order.

quizTarget: Replace -1 with c(-1,2). What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: values[-1] selects all entries except the first. It does not mean the final element as it does in some languages.
A zero index contributes no selected element. It can appear with negative indices without selecting anything.
A subscript vector containing both a positive and a negative nonzero index is rejected. Choose either selection or omission consistently.

reasoning: The requested subscript mixes incompatible selection styles instead of identifying a valid subset.

quizTarget: Add the explicit !is.na(values) & check to the mask. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A mask from values > 2 selects elements whose comparison is TRUE. A comparison involving NA normally produces NA.
Indexing an atomic vector with an NA mask entry includes a missing result at that position. Unknown does not silently mean false.

is.na(values) marks missing entries. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.

reasoning: The combined mask is FALSE at the missing position and TRUE only for the known qualifying value.

quizTarget: Change the requested name from "b" to "x". What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: names(values) <- c("a","b") labels the two positions. Labels do not alter their stored numeric values.
values["b"] selects the entry named b. A name is not the same thing as its position number.
For this bracket lookup, an absent name produces NA. Do not assume a misspelled name selects the first entry.

reasoning: The requested label is absent, so this atomic-vector lookup produces a missing result.

quizTarget: Replace is.na with is.finite. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: NA represents missing information. NaN represents an undefined numeric result. Inf and -Inf represent positive and negative infinity.
is.na is TRUE for NA and NaN, but FALSE for Inf and ordinary finite values. Comparing a value with NA does not establish whether it is missing.
is.finite is TRUE only for finite numeric values, so it is FALSE for NA, NaN and infinities.

reasoning: The finite-value predicate excludes missing, undefined and infinite numeric values.

quizTarget: Replace NULL with NA. What length prints?

essentialSupport.fact: NULL is a special null object with length zero. NA is a missing value that can occupy an element position.
numeric(0) creates an empty double vector, whereas character(0) creates empty text storage. Both have length zero but are not identical types.
length reports how many entries an object contains; it is not the amount of text used to print the object.

reasoning: NA is a length-one missing value here, unlike the length-zero NULL object.

quizTarget: Add collapse="|" to the paste0 call. What length prints?

essentialSupport.fact: c("a","b") contains two text elements, not a single string with a comma.
paste0("item", c(1,2)) produces two character elements: item1 and item2. Numeric values are converted to text for this operation.
collapse="|" joins the resulting elements with a vertical bar. Without collapse, the result can still contain several strings.

reasoning: collapse combines the result entries into a single character element; length counts elements, not characters.

quizTarget: Change items[1] to items[[1]]. What type prints?

essentialSupport.fact: list(score=7, topic="stars") stores a number and text as separate components without forcing one common atomic type.
items[1] returns a one-component list. items[[1]] extracts the component itself. That extracted component can be a vector or another complex object.
items$score is convenient for a fixed component name. For programmatically supplied exact names, [[ with an explicit name is clearer than relying on partial matching.

reasoning: The first component is the numeric literal 7, stored as a double; [[ removes the selected outer list level.

quizTarget: Change the requested row to 2 while keeping the score column. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: data.frame(topic=c("a","b"), score=c(2,4)) combines two columns. Columns may have different types while each describes the same number of rows.
frame[1, "score"] selects row 1 from the score column. An empty row position means all rows; row and column positions are not interchangeable.
frame$score extracts that column. A row normally combines observations across several columns, rather than being a single variable.

reasoning: Both row and column selectors contribute to the result; the column stays score and the row changes.

quizTarget: Remove drop=FALSE. What class prints for this numeric column?

essentialSupport.fact: Selecting one data-frame column with frame[, "score"] normally simplifies to the underlying vector.
frame[, "score", drop=FALSE] keeps a one-column data frame. The values are the same, but the container shape differs.
A function expecting row/column structure can behave differently when given a vector. Do not infer shape only from the printed numbers.

reasoning: The default subset behavior drops the one-column data-frame structure in this expression.

quizTarget: Convert to character before numeric: as.numeric(as.character(value)). What prints for these labels?

essentialSupport.fact: factor(c("20","10"), levels=c("10","20")) stores category labels with integer codes determined by the level order.
as.numeric(factor_value) exposes the underlying category codes. It does not parse the printed category labels as numbers.
as.character first obtains the labels. as.numeric can then parse valid numeric text; unsuitable text can produce NA with a warning, so real input still needs validation.

reasoning: The intermediate character conversion obtains the displayed labels, separating label parsing from category-code access.

quizTarget: Add byrow=TRUE when creating the matrix. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: matrix(c(1,2,3,4), nrow=2) creates a two-row matrix. An array generalizes dimensions beyond rows and columns.
With byrow=FALSE, the first column receives 1 and 2, then the second receives 3 and 4. byrow=TRUE fills rows instead.
m[1,2] reads row 1, column 2. Changing the fill order changes where input values are placed, not the meaning of the two indices.

reasoning: Row-wise filling places 2 at row 1, column 2.

quizTarget: Replace values with numeric(0). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: for (index in seq_along(values)) visits each valid position of this vector. It does not require a separate manual counter update.
seq_along(numeric(0)) is an empty index sequence. The colon operator makes a sequence including both endpoints. Thus 1:length(values) becomes 1:0 for empty input, which is not an empty sequence.
numeric(length(values)) can allocate a result vector before a loop. Avoid repeatedly growing large vectors without measuring the cost.
count <- count + 1 updates the local count once per iteration. The starting zero remains zero if the sequence is empty.

reasoning: seq_along avoids the empty-input trap of 1:length and produces no iterations.

quizTarget: Supply offset=-1 as an additional named argument. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: function(score, offset=1) declares a required score and a default offset. Named arguments can be supplied explicitly rather than relying on position.
The last evaluated expression supplies the result unless return exits earlier. Returning a value is distinct from printing it.
R supports several argument-matching rules, including partial matching in some situations. Exact names are clearer and less vulnerable to future parameter additions.

reasoning: The function evaluates 3 plus the supplied -1 rather than using the omitted-argument default.

quizTarget: Remove the inner value <- 9 assignment. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A function can read a value from the environment where it was created when no local binding shadows it. This is lexical lookup, not a search through every caller’s local variables.
value <- 9 in this function does not automatically overwrite the outer value. The super-assignment operator <<- has different effects and is not used here.
The function returns its final local value. cat prints that result followed by the outer value, separated by a comma.

reasoning: Without a local value binding, lookup reaches the outer environment; reading it does not modify it.
